overview: Speed and focus is the ability to scan information quickly and pick out the right item without getting distracted. Many IQ tests set strict time limits, so practising fast recognition of the largest, smallest or odd item builds the rhythm you need on test day.

strategy.b: Glance across the whole row once before you commit to an answer. A quick first sweep finds the candidates, and a second look confirms them, which is faster than checking each option in turn.
Memorise the core rules, such as the multiples of three and how place value orders numbers. Recognition is faster when you do not have to work the rule out from scratch every time.
Cross out options that clearly break the rule, then compare the survivors. Removing two or three answers cuts the work in half and keeps your decision quick.
Keep your eyes on the item in front of you and let the timer run. Glancing at the clock costs seconds, and a steady pace beats a rushed one full of avoidable errors.

fig.title: Scan for the largest
fig.note: The highlighted cell holds the largest value.

drills.name: Largest number
drills.how: Scan the whole set once to find the biggest value, checking the leading digit first. A number with more digits is usually larger, so compare the length before you compare digits in the same position.
drills.tip: Compare leading digits first, and only look further when they match.
drills.mistake: Comparing the last digit first, which can make 81 look bigger than 92 when it is not. Fix it by reading the leading digit first, so 92 wins because 9 is larger than 8.

ex.q: Which is the largest of 73, 46, 81 and 29?
ex.why: Compare leading digits: 8 is the highest, so 81 is the largest, and 73 is close but its leading digit is only 7.

drills.name: Smallest number
drills.how: Scan for the lowest value by checking the leading digit, then the length. A number with fewer digits is usually smaller, so look at the shortest values first.
drills.tip: Treat the leading digit as the main clue, and only compare the rest when two numbers tie.
drills.mistake: Picking the number with the smallest last digit, which ignores place value. Fix it by comparing the leading digit first, so 12 is smaller than 40 even though 0 is smaller than 2.

ex.q: Which is the smallest of 91, 58, 37 and 23?
ex.why: The leading digits are 9, 5, 3 and 2, and 2 is the lowest, so 23 is the smallest.

drills.name: Multiples of three
drills.how: Check whether a number is a multiple of three by adding its digits. If the digit total is a multiple of three, so is the number, which lets you sort a list quickly.
drills.tip: Add the digits in pairs in your head, and remember that a total of 3, 6 or 9 is always a yes.
drills.mistake: Checking the last digit instead of the digit total, which misses numbers such as 21 or 33. Fix it by adding the digits every time: 2 plus 1 is 3, so 21 is a multiple of three.

ex.q: Which of 16, 27, 34 and 50 is a multiple of three?
ex.why: Add the digits of 27: 2 plus 7 is 9, which is a multiple of three, so 27 qualifies.

drills.name: Odd one out
drills.how: Work out the rule shared by most of the items, then find the one that breaks it. Check simple properties first, such as odd or even, multiples, or size, and only then look for subtler patterns.
drills.tip: Say the shared rule in a single word before you look at the options.
drills.mistake: Choosing the item that looks different rather than the one that breaks the rule. Fix it by testing each item against the rule so you do not pick by visual oddness.

ex.q: Which is the odd one out of 12, 18, 25 and 30?
ex.why: 12, 18 and 30 are all even multiples of three, while 25 is odd and not a multiple of three.

drills.name: Wide field
drills.how: Six numbers appear for a shorter time than usual, so you must lock onto the target rule straight away. Decide the rule before the numbers appear, then scan in one pass and commit to the first match you are sure of.
drills.tip: Read the question first, then look, so your eyes know what to find.
drills.mistake: Looking at the numbers before reading the question, which wastes the short window. Fix it by reading the rule first, then scanning with one target in mind.

ex.q: Six numbers flash for one second: 3, 17, 8, 25, 40 and 11. Which is the largest?
ex.why: 40 is the highest of the six values, so it is the largest number shown.

levels: Level 1: Pick the largest or smallest of four two-digit numbers with no time limit.
Level 2: Find the largest or smallest among six numbers within ten seconds.
Level 3: Spot the multiples of three among eight numbers in under eight seconds.
Level 4: Identify the odd one out from four items in under five seconds.
Level 5: Scan six numbers in four seconds and report the largest or smallest.
Level 6: Scan six numbers in one second while holding the rule in mind without rereading the question.
routine: Day 1: Spend five minutes on largest and smallest checks with two-digit numbers, timing each set.
Day 2: Spend ten minutes on multiples of three, adding the digits to confirm every answer.
Day 3: Practise odd one out, saying the shared rule aloud before you choose.
Day 4: Practise wide field with six numbers, shortening the viewing time once you reach nine correct in ten.
Day 5: Mix all five drills for one set, note your slowest drill, and open next week with it.
